1.title: Act 1 — Philadelphia, 1764
1.subtitle: The Founding Mind That Shouldn't Be
1.intro: Philadelphia, 1764. The city smells of ink, river water and woodsmoke. Something is wrong here: Benjamin Franklin — printer, thinker, experimenter — has begun speaking of devices no one in this century could know. Find what changed, prove it, and repair it before the distortion spreads.
1.anomaly: A portable music player hums on Franklin's workbench — an object from the late 20th century, two hundred years too early.

2.title: Act 2 — Manchester, 1830s
2.subtitle: The Machine That Arrived Too Early
2.intro: Manchester, England, in the 1830s. The mills never sleep. But inside Grimshaw's textile mill, a machine hums that should not exist for another seventy years — and the workers' stories do not agree about when it arrived.
2.anomaly: A small radio receiver crackles in the mill — a device from the 20th century, decades too early.

3.title: Act 3 — Europe, 1690s
3.subtitle: The Discovery Out of Time
3.intro: Europe, in the last years of the 17th century. Scholars argue by candlelight over the new philosophy. But a chart on the apothecary's wall shows a theory of disease that no one alive could have proven — the chain of discovery has been broken.
3.anomaly: A germ-theory chart hangs in the apothecary — correct, and two centuries too early.

4.title: Act 4 — An Airfield, 1912
4.subtitle: The Aircraft That Changed History
4.intro: An airfield in the early years of powered flight. Canvas, wood, wire and courage. But in the hangar, a turbine blade gleams — metal from the jet age, fitted to a machine of wood and linen.
4.anomaly: A jet turbine blade is bolted to a 1912 biplane — technology from the 1940s, thirty years too early.

5.title: Act 5 — The Temporal Core
5.subtitle: Who Changed History?
5.intro: Outside normal time, the Temporal Core turns. Every anomaly you repaired left a trace here. The Chronarch — custodian of the timelines — has been waiting for you. The cause of the disturbances is finally within reach.
5.anomaly: The Core itself is fractured: four key digits, one from each act you repaired, will seal it.

workshop.name: Franklin's Workshop
workshop.caption: A workbench crowded with tools, jars and papers — and something that does not belong.
workshop.desc: Franklin's workshop. Glass jars, copper wire, a Leyden jar and scattered notes cover the bench. A small black device hums softly where no device should hum.

hotspots.name: Humming Device
hotspots.desc: A small black rectangle with a glowing screen. It plays music no instrument in 1764 could make. It is the anomaly — handle it with care.

hotspots.name: The Cluttered Workbench
hotspots.desc: A clutter of tools and devices. Somewhere here are objects that do not belong in 1764.

hotspots.name: Magnifying Glass
hotspots.desc: A brass magnifying glass, left beside a stack of letters.

hotspots.name: Leyden Jar
hotspots.desc: A glass jar lined with metal foil — Franklin's electrical storage jar. FACT: the Leyden jar was invented in 1745–46 and Franklin used it in his electrical experiments.

hotspots.name: Benjamin Franklin
hotspots.desc: Benjamin Franklin, printer and natural philosopher, frowning at the humming device.

hotspots.name: Workbench Notes
hotspots.desc: Notes in Franklin's hand about electricity — and a sketch of the humming device, drawn as if he had seen it in a dream.

printshop.name: Printing Shop
printshop.caption: The press groans, the type is set, and the smell of fresh ink fills the air.
printshop.desc: Franklin's printing shop. The great press dominates the room. Trays of movable type, ink balls and paper stacks surround it.

hotspots.name: Printing Press
hotspots.desc: A wooden screw press. FACT: Franklin ran a successful printing business in Philadelphia from 1728, publishing the Pennsylvania Gazette from 1729.

hotspots.name: Abel Crowe, Master Printer
hotspots.desc: Abel Crowe, the master printer, wiping ink from his hands. He has worked this press for twenty years.

hotspots.name: Spool of Copper Wire
hotspots.desc: A spool of fine copper wire, used for electrical experiments.

hotspots.name: Ink Pot
hotspots.desc: A pot of thick black printing ink.

marketplace.name: Marketplace
marketplace.caption: Stalls of bread, cloth and iron — and one stall selling something impossible.
marketplace.desc: The Philadelphia marketplace. Vendors call out their wares. One stall displays a strange, clear bottle that catches the light oddly.

hotspots.name: Silas Green, Vendor
hotspots.desc: Silas Green sells iron goods and oddities. He is cheerful, talkative, and knows more than he lets on.

hotspots.name: Lodestone
hotspots.desc: A dark, heavy stone that pulls iron to itself. FACT: lodestones — naturally magnetic rock — have been known for thousands of years.

hotspots.name: Clear Bottle
hotspots.desc: A perfectly clear, feather-light bottle. No glassblower in 1764 could make this. It is a distortion.

hotspots.name: Tom Beck, Apprentice
hotspots.desc: Tom Beck, Franklin's young apprentice, carrying a bundle of freshly printed sheets.

library.name: Library Company
library.caption: Shelves of books, the smell of old paper, and a librarian who misses nothing.
library.desc: The Library Company of Philadelphia. FACT: founded by Franklin in 1731, it was America's first lending library. The librarian guards its collection fiercely.

hotspots.name: Prudence Hale, Librarian
hotspots.desc: Prudence Hale, librarian of the Library Company. She notices every book out of place — and every fact out of time.

hotspots.name: Glass Tube
hotspots.desc: A slender glass tube from the instrument cabinet, used in electrical demonstrations.

hotspots.name: Glowing Lamp
hotspots.desc: A glass bulb glowing without flame or oil. FACT: practical electric lamps did not exist until Edison's work in 1879 — more than a century from now.

hotspots.name: Book Shelves
hotspots.desc: Rows of bound volumes: philosophy, natural history, law. The library's catalogue is meticulous.

hotspots.name: A Timeline of Franklin's Life
hotspots.desc: A chart of Franklin's milestones on the wall. Some of them are out of order.

street.name: Philadelphia Street
street.caption: Cobblestones, carriages and townsfolk — the city going about its day.
street.desc: A Philadelphia street in 1764. Carriages rattle over cobblestones. A notice board carries the day's proclamations.

hotspots.name: Notice Board
hotspots.desc: Posted notices: a lost dog, a meeting of the Philosophical Society, and a warning about a 'strange humming' heard near the workshop.

hotspots.name: Candle Stall
hotspots.desc: A stall selling tallow candles — the honest light of 1764.

hotspots.name: Kite Sketch
hotspots.desc: A child's kite, painted with a key. FACT: Franklin's famous kite experiment of 1752 showed lightning is electricity — but he did not fly the kite alone in a storm to 'discover' electricity, and he was not struck by lightning.

meeting.name: Meeting Room
meeting.caption: A quiet room where the city's thinkers gather to argue — politely, mostly.
meeting.desc: The meeting room of the Philosophical Society. A long table, chairs, a globe, and a locked document box.

hotspots.name: Document Box
hotspots.desc: A locked box of society papers. It opens with a brass key.
hotspots.lockedMsg: The box is locked. It needs a brass key — the notice board in the street mentioned one lost near the market.

hotspots.name: Sealing Wax
hotspots.desc: Sticks of red sealing wax for letters and documents.

hotspots.name: Brass Compass
hotspots.desc: A brass compass, its needle steady and true.

hotspots.name: Terrestrial Globe
hotspots.desc: A globe showing the known world of 1764 — the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia, with vast blank spaces still unmapped.

mill.name: Grimshaw's Textile Mill
mill.caption: Looms thunder, belts spin, and a small radio crackles where no radio should be.
mill.desc: The mill floor. Power looms clatter in rows. In the corner, behind a loom, a small wooden box crackles with voices from nowhere.

hotspots.name: Crackling Box
hotspots.desc: A wooden box with a glowing dial, speaking in voices. FACT: radio broadcasting did not exist until the early 20th century — this is a distortion.

hotspots.name: Josiah Grimshaw, Mill Owner
hotspots.desc: Josiah Grimshaw, owner of the mill. Proud of his machines, nervous about the strange box.

hotspots.name: Wrench
hotspots.desc: A heavy iron wrench, used on the looms.

hotspots.name: Power Loom
hotspots.desc: A power loom. FACT: Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom in 1785; by the 1830s, steam-driven looms filled Manchester's mills.

hotspots.name: The Mill's Work Chart
hotspots.desc: A chart shows the stages of cloth-making — but the order has been scrambled.

cottage.name: Worker's Cottage
cottage.caption: A small cottage, a tired family, and three different stories about the box.
cottage.desc: The Fletcher cottage. Tommy Fletcher, a mill worker, sits by the fire with his family. Three people here will tell you three different stories about the crackling box.

hotspots.name: Tommy Fletcher, Mill Worker
hotspots.desc: Tommy Fletcher, who has worked the looms since he was a boy. He was there the night the box arrived.

hotspots.name: The Workers' Accounts
hotspots.desc: Three workers describe the same night. Their stories do not agree.

hotspots.name: Oil Can
hotspots.desc: A can of machine oil.

hotspots.name: Cotton Bale
hotspots.desc: A bale of raw cotton from across the Atlantic. FACT: Manchester's mills ran on cotton grown largely by enslaved labour in the Americas — the industry's wealth had a human cost.

warehouse.name: Canal Warehouse
warehouse.caption: Barges, bales and ledgers — the paperwork of an empire of cloth.
warehouse.desc: The canal warehouse. Barges unload cotton; ledgers record every bale. The engineer Eliza Hart is checking a delivery.

hotspots.name: Eliza Hart, Mill Engineer
hotspots.desc: Eliza Hart, the mill's engineer. She understands machines better than anyone in Manchester — and she knows the box is impossible.

hotspots.name: Loom Shuttle
hotspots.desc: A wooden shuttle, worn smooth by years of weaving.

hotspots.name: Delivery Ledger
hotspots.desc: A ledger of deliveries. The entries stop making sense the week the box appeared.

hotspots.name: Copper Wire
hotspots.desc: A coil of copper wire among the spare parts.

observatory.name: Observatory Tower
observatory.caption: Brass, glass and starlight — the new science of the heavens.
observatory.desc: The observatory tower. A great brass telescope points at the night sky. Master Corvin charts the planets by candlelight.

hotspots.name: Master Corvin, Astronomer
hotspots.desc: Master Corvin, astronomer. He has read Newton and argues about comets with anyone who will listen.

hotspots.name: Brass Telescope
hotspots.desc: A long brass telescope. FACT: telescopes transformed astronomy in the 1600s; Newton's reflecting telescope dates to 1668.

hotspots.name: Star Chart
hotspots.desc: A hand-drawn chart of the planets, carefully inked.

hotspots.name: Sealing Wax
hotspots.desc: Sealing wax for letters to fellow scholars.

apothecary.name: The Apothecary
apothecary.caption: Herbs, jars and a chart that knows too much.
apothecary.desc: The apothecary's shop. Jars of herbs line the walls. On the wall hangs a chart describing tiny creatures causing disease — drawn with impossible precision.

hotspots.name: Germ-Theory Chart
hotspots.desc: A chart showing tiny creatures causing disease, with cures listed beside them. FACT: germ theory was not proven until the 1860s — this chart is two centuries too early.

hotspots.name: Sister Agnes, Apothecary
hotspots.desc: Sister Agnes, apothecary and healer. She hung the chart herself — she swears she copied it from a book that no longer exists.

hotspots.name: Ink Pot
hotspots.desc: A pot of iron-gall ink.

hotspots.name: Simple Microscope
hotspots.desc: A simple microscope. FACT: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes of the 1670s revealed tiny living things — but no one then connected them to disease.

hotspots.name: The Traveller's Letter
hotspots.desc: A coded letter left by the pedlar. The code looks simple — a letter shift.

university.name: University Hall
university.caption: Scholars debate the new philosophy — and one student asks the right question.
university.desc: The university hall. Candlelit desks, disputed theses, and Pieter, a student who has noticed that the discoveries are arriving in the wrong order.

hotspots.name: Pieter, Student
hotspots.desc: Pieter, a student of natural philosophy. He has listed the great discoveries on a slate — and the order troubles him.

hotspots.name: Bound Manuscript
hotspots.desc: A bound manuscript of lecture notes, ready for correction.

hotspots.name: Quill Pen
hotspots.desc: A goose-quill pen, freshly cut.

hotspots.name: Principia Volume
hotspots.desc: A copy of Newton's Principia. FACT: published in 1687, it set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.

hotspots.name: The Scholar's Slate
hotspots.desc: Four great discoveries are chalked on a slate — in the wrong order.

airfield.name: The Airfield
airfield.caption: Wind, canvas and the smell of castor oil — flight is barely nine years old.
airfield.desc: The airfield. A biplane stands on the grass, its propeller turning lazily in the wind. Captain Mallory is preparing for a test flight.

hotspots.name: Captain Rose Mallory, Pilot
hotspots.desc: Captain Rose Mallory, pilot. She has flown in wind, rain and fog — and she refuses to fly a machine she does not trust.

hotspots.name: Biplane
hotspots.desc: A wood-and-linen biplane. FACT: the Wright brothers first flew a powered aeroplane in 1903; by 1912, biplanes were crossing channels and carrying mail.

hotspots.name: Flight Log
hotspots.desc: The airfield's flight log, recording every takeoff and landing.

hotspots.name: Spark Plug
hotspots.desc: A spare spark plug for the rotary engine.

hotspots.name: The Assembly Notes
hotspots.desc: A fitter's notes on building an aeroplane — the steps are jumbled.

hangar.name: The Hangar
hangar.caption: Tools, oil and canvas — and a blade that belongs to another age.
hangar.desc: The hangar. Workbenches, engine parts and a half-built wing. Bolted to the biplane's nose is a blade of strange, gleaming metal.

hotspots.name: Turbine Blade
hotspots.desc: A curved metal blade, light and impossibly strong. FACT: jet turbine engines were developed in the late 1930s and 1940s — this blade is thirty years too early.

hotspots.name: Gus Berger, Mechanic
hotspots.desc: Gus Berger, mechanic. He fitted the blade himself — he swears it arrived in a crate with no sender.

hotspots.name: Wrench
hotspots.desc: A heavy wrench, sized for engine bolts.

hotspots.name: Linen Fabric Roll
hotspots.desc: A roll of linen fabric for covering wings.

hotspots.name: The Parts Bench
hotspots.desc: A jumble of aircraft parts. Some are authentic 1912 parts; some are impostors.

office.name: Hangar Office
office.caption: Blueprints, telegrams and a crate with no sender.
office.desc: The hangar office. Blueprints cover the desk. A crate stands in the corner — its label is blank where a sender's name should be.

hotspots.name: Clara Webb, Engineer
hotspots.desc: Clara Webb, aeronautical engineer. She has done the sums: the blade cannot work on this airframe, and yet the machine flew.

hotspots.name: Biplane Blueprint
hotspots.desc: The biplane's blueprint. Every part is accounted for — except the blade.

hotspots.name: Box of Rivets
hotspots.desc: A box of steel rivets.

hotspots.name: Spare Propeller Blade
hotspots.desc: A wooden propeller blade, carved and balanced by hand.

core.name: The Temporal Core
core.caption: A chamber outside time, where the repaired past glows like stars.
core.desc: The Temporal Core. Streams of light — each one a timeline you repaired — flow into a great fractured ring. The fracture pulses with the last of the distortion.

hotspots.name: The Fracture
hotspots.desc: The fracture in the Core. Four key digits — one from each act you repaired — will seal it.

hotspots.name: The Chronarch
hotspots.desc: The Chronarch, custodian of the timelines. Neither young nor old, neither kind nor cruel — only patient.

hotspots.name: Stream of 1764
hotspots.desc: A stream of light: Philadelphia, 1764, steady and bright since your repair.

gallery.name: Memory Gallery
gallery.caption: Every choice you made, kept as light.
gallery.desc: The Memory Gallery. The Core shows you your own journey: the moments you chose well, and the moments you did not.

hotspots.name: Memory: Franklin
hotspots.desc: A memory of Philadelphia. What you told Franklin echoes here.

hotspots.name: Memory: The Mill
hotspots.desc: A memory of Manchester. The workers' voices still argue.

hotspots.name: Chronarch's Sigil
hotspots.desc: A small sigil left by the Chronarch. Take it — you will need proof of your deeds.

dais.name: The Dais
dais.caption: The Chronarch's dais. The final reckoning waits here.
dais.desc: The Dais. The Chronarch stands ready to hear your final report. When the Core is sealed, the timeline will be judged.

hotspots.name: The Chronarch
hotspots.desc: The Chronarch, waiting. 'Speak, Restorer. What did you learn?'

hotspots.name: The Final Seal
hotspots.desc: The seal that will close the Core — once the fracture is repaired and the final quiz is passed.
hotspots.lockedMsg: The seal is inert. The Core's fracture must be repaired first.

n1.text: Franklin looks up from the humming device. “You carry yourself like a person out of their century, friend. That box sings, and I cannot say how. Tell me — what do you make of it?”

choices.text: “It is a scientific instrument. Best left alone.”
choices.response: Franklin nods slowly. “A cautious answer. Caution is a virtue I have come to respect.” He sets the device down and steps back from it.

choices.text: “It is from the future. Two hundred years from now.”
choices.response: Franklin's eyes widen — and then, dangerously, they gleam. “The future! Then tell me everything. What wonders come? What machines? What knowledge?” The device hums louder, as if pleased.
“The marketplace?” Franklin frowns. “Then someone in this city is selling tomorrow. That is a trade I would like to understand — and stop.”
You study him carefully. He is a man of his time — ink on his fingers, curiosity in his eyes. The distortion is the device, not the man.

n2.text: “The device is not of this age, I am certain of that much,” Franklin says. “I have spent my life studying electricity, and this box holds lightning in a way I do not understand. If you can silence it without harming my workshop, I will help you however I can.”

choices.text: “I need to build a resonator — wire, lodestone and glass.”
choices.response: “Wire I have. Lodestone you will find in the market. Glass tubing, in the library's instrument cabinet. Build it, and I will hold the door against interruption.”
“Ah — the kite. In 1752 I showed that lightning is electricity. Some say I flew it in a storm alone; I did not. My son William stood with me, and we were careful. History will embroider the rest.”

n3.text: “The future!” Franklin laughs, delighted. “Do they fly? Do they speak across oceans without wires? Tell me one thing — only one — and I shall keep it safe.”

choices.text: Refuse. “Some knowledge must wait for its own time.”
choices.response: Franklin studies you for a long moment, then nods. “You are right, of course. A seed planted in winter rots. I shall forget what I have guessed.” The device dims slightly.
“Light without flame!” Franklin breathes. “I shall think of nothing else for a month.” The distortion in the room deepens — the lamp in the library begins to glow of its own accord.

n1.text: Abel Crowe wipes his hands on his apron. “Thirty years at this press, friend. I know every squeak of it. But this week the press has started printing words I never set — words about machines that fly and voices in boxes.”

choices.response: He shows you a proof sheet: the words are English, but they speak of a world of 'broadcasts' and 'batteries'. “I never set this type,” he says, pale. “I would swear it on the press itself.”
“A pedlar, last Tuesday. Sold Franklin a box that hums. I told him not to buy it. Printers know: some bargains cost more than coin.”

n2.text: “If you can put this right, do it quietly,” Crowe says. “A printer's reputation is his livelihood. And take this — spare type, in case your work needs letters set.”

choices.response: You take a small tray of movable type. It may prove useful.
“Discretion,” Crowe says approvingly, “is the better part of printing.”

n1.text: Silas Green spreads his hands wide. “Iron goods! Honest iron! And — for a discerning customer — curiosities from far away. A pedlar brought me that clear bottle. Pretty thing, is it not?”

choices.response: “Gone west, two days past. He sold the bottle, a humming box to Franklin, and a lamp to the library — then vanished like smoke. Odd fellow. Paid in coins I had never seen.”

choices.text: “That bottle is not glass. It is not of this century.”
choices.response: Green laughs, then stops when he sees your face. “Not glass? Then what is it? …You know, it never did feel right in the hand. Too light. Too perfect.”

n2.text: “Take the lodestone, friend,” Green says, pressing the dark stone into your hand. “If you are chasing a pedlar who sells tomorrow, you will want something that points true.”

choices.response: The lodestone is heavy and cool. It tugs gently at your compass.

choices.text: “Keep your eyes open for the pedlar.”
choices.response: “Always,” Green says. “A vendor remembers every face. If he comes back, I will send word.”

n1.text: Tom Beck shifts his bundle of printed sheets. “Mr. Franklin has been strange all week, sir. He hums tunes nobody taught him. And he asked me if I knew what a 'recording' was. I did not know what to say.”

choices.text: “You did well to notice. Keep watching him.”
choices.response: Tom stands a little straighter. “I will, sir. Someone should.”
Tom hums a few bars — a melody that will not be written for two hundred years. It raises the hairs on your neck.

n1.text: Prudence Hale does not look up from her catalogue. “The lamp appeared on Tuesday. No one brought it. No one shelved it. It simply was there, glowing. I have catalogued it under 'Impossibilities'.”

choices.response: “You may — if you promise to return everything to its place. A library is a machine for finding things, young person, and it only works when everything is where it belongs.”

choices.text: “What do you know about the pedlar?”
choices.response: “He asked for books about the future. I told him the future has not been written yet. He laughed and said, 'Not in this library.'”

n2.text: “The Library Company was founded in 1731,” she says, “so that knowledge might be shared. What you are hunting is knowledge in the wrong place at the wrong time. That is the worst kind of mis-shelving.”

choices.response: “See that you do,” she says, and slides a glass tube across the desk. “You will need this. Do not break it.”

n1.text: Grimshaw puffs out his chest. “My mill is the most modern in Manchester, sir. Steam power, power looms, two hundred hands. And now — this box. It speaks, sir. It speaks in voices from London, or so it claims, with no wires at all.”

choices.response: “Tuesday last. A pedlar sold it to my foreman — said it was a 'wireless'. I had it put behind the looms so the hands would not be distracted. The hands are distracted anyway.”

choices.text: “The box is impossible. It must be removed.”
choices.response: “Impossible or not, it cost me five pounds,” Grimshaw grumbles. “But if it frightens my workers, it goes. You may take it once it is silenced — I want no more of it.”

n2.text: “Eliza Hart, my engineer, has examined it,” Grimshaw says. “She says it cannot work, and yet it works. Talk to her — she is at the warehouse. And mind the belts.”

choices.response: “Do. She is the cleverest person in this mill, myself included.”

n1.text: Tommy Fletcher stares into the fire. “I was there the night it came, sir. Three of us saw it. But ask us separately and you will hear three different nights.”

choices.response: “A man with a cart, after midnight. He carried the box into the mill himself. I asked where he was from and he said — 'from later'. I thought he meant later that night.”

choices.text: “Did the others see the same man?”
choices.response: “Martha says she saw a woman. Old Jeb says he saw no one at all, only the box, already there in the morning. One of us is wrong — or the night itself was.”

n2.text: “The box talks of a world where the mills are silent,” Tommy says quietly. “I do not know if that frightens me or gives me hope.”

choices.text: “The mills will change — but not like this, not yet.”
choices.response: Tommy nods. “Then put it right, sir. For all our sakes.”

n1.text: Eliza Hart does not look up from her drawings. “The box receives voices through the air. I have tested it. There is no wire, no tube, no trick I can find. By every law of natural philosophy I know, it cannot exist.”

choices.response: “Its heart is a coil of some kind. Ground it — drain its charge into the earth through copper — and it should go quiet. I have copper wire in the warehouse, and a wrench in the mill.”

choices.text: “Could it be a trick — ventriloquism, a hidden wire?”
choices.response: “I checked for wires myself, in the dark, with a candle. There are none. I dislike mysteries, sir. I dislike them very much.”

n2.text: “One more thing,” Hart says. “The loom sequence matters. Raw cotton, carding, spinning, weaving — in that order, always. Whoever built this mill's future forgot that machines obey order. Remember it.”

choices.response: “Good. Now go and put the future back where it belongs.”

n1.text: Master Corvin gestures at the stars. “Newton showed us the laws in 1687 — the Principia, the greatest book of our age. And yet a chart in the apothecary claims knowledge of creatures no eye has truly seen. Order, friend. Discovery has an order, and someone has broken it.”

choices.text: “What is the correct order of the great discoveries?”
choices.response: “Harvey showed the blood's circulation in 1628. Boyle his law of airs in 1662. Leeuwenhoek his tiny creatures in the 1670s. Newton his Principia in 1687. Each stands on the last. Remove one stone and the arch falls.”
“Newton's reflecting telescope, 1668 — a mirror instead of a lens, and the heavens opened. Without it, we would still be squinting through coloured glass.”

n2.text: “The apothecary's chart must be corrected, not burned,” Corvin says. “Knowledge is not the enemy — timing is. Write the correction, seal it, and place it where the false chart hangs.”

choices.response: “Then you will need ink, a manuscript and wax. The apothecary has ink; the university has paper; I have wax. Go.”

n1.text: Sister Agnes wrings her hands. “I copied the chart from a book, I swear it. A traveller left the book here — it described tiny creatures and their cures in perfect detail. When I went to show my sisters, the book was gone. Only my copy remains.”

choices.text: “The book described germs — a theory two centuries early.”
choices.response: “Two centuries?” She pales. “Then I have hung a lie on my wall, even if the lie is true. Take it down, I beg you — but write the truth in its place, so the next healer is not misled.”
“A pedlar, with a cart of oddities. He paid for his herbs in coins no mint I know has struck.”

n2.text: “The chart is written in a cipher, did you notice?” Agnes says. “The traveller's note at the bottom — letters shifted, like a child's puzzle. I could never read it.”

choices.response: “Then you are cleverer than I. The letters march three places forward, I think — a Caesar's trick, if my Latin serves.”

n1.text: Pieter shows you his slate. Four discoveries, written in a row — but the order is wrong, and he knows it. “Harvey, Boyle, Leeuwenhoek, Newton,” he says. “Or is it Newton first? My master says the order matters more than the dates.”

choices.text: “The order is: Harvey, Boyle, Leeuwenhoek, Newton.”
choices.response: Pieter beams. “Yes! Each discovery rests on the one before. Harvey's blood, Boyle's air, Leeuwenhoek's tiny creatures, Newton's laws. You understand!”

choices.text: “Let me look at your slate more closely.”
choices.response: The slate lists the discoveries with dates: Harvey 1628, Boyle 1662, Leeuwenhoek 1670s, Newton 1687. The chain is clear once you see the years.

n2.text: “If you fix the chart,” Pieter says, “promise me you will also fix the slate. I want to learn the true order — not the broken one.”

choices.response: “Then here — take my quill. You will need a steady hand for the correction.”

n1.text: Captain Mallory folds her arms. “Nine years since the Wrights flew, and already people want miracles. That blade on my machine — it is no propeller I know. It is too light, too strong, and it hums at a pitch that sets my teeth on edge.”

choices.text: “What does the blade do to the machine?”
choices.response: “It makes her fly too fast and too far, and the wings were never built for it. Gus fitted it. Clara did the sums. We all agree: it does not belong.”

choices.text: “Have you flown with the blade fitted?”
choices.response: “Once. Never again. The machine shuddered like a living thing, and the airspeed needle went where no needle should go. I landed and walked away, and I do not walk away from much.”

n2.text: “Remove it properly,” Mallory says. “Wrench, patience, and the right order: frame, wings, engine, propeller. Machines are built in order, and they are unbuilt in order.”

choices.response: “Good. And when it is done, I will fly her properly — the way she was meant to fly.”

n1.text: Gus Berger wipes grease from his hands. “The blade came in a crate, no sender, no papers. It fitted the hub like it was made for it — which is the strangest part, because no one here made it.”

choices.response: “With the right wrench, yes. But the bolts are strange — they need patience, not force. And the blade must come off before the propeller goes back on, or the balance will be wrong.”
“A pedlar, of all people. A cart, a smile, and coins from no country I know. He said the blade was 'from later'. I thought he meant later that week.”

n2.text: “Here,” Gus says, handing you a wrench. “It is the one I use for engine bolts. Bring me the blade when it is off, and I will see it melted down myself.”

choices.response: The wrench is heavy and honest.

n1.text: Clara Webb spreads her calculations across the desk. “Lift must exceed weight. Thrust must exceed drag. The blade gives thrust the airframe cannot bear — the numbers do not lie, even when the machine flies.”

choices.response: “Wood, linen, wire and a rotary engine. The propeller is carved wood. The wings are fabric over spruce. Anything of gleaming alloy and impossible lightness does not belong.”
“The wings will fail in flight, or the machine will outrun its own design and tear itself apart. Either way, someone dies — and history remembers a disaster instead of a triumph.”

n2.text: “The blueprint is on the desk,” Clara says. “Study it. When you know what belongs, you will know what does not.”

choices.response: “Good. Knowledge first, tools second. That is the whole of engineering.”

n1.text: The Chronarch regards you with eyes like distant stars. “You repaired four timelines, Restorer. Each time, the same hand: a pedlar with a cart of impossibilities, selling tomorrow to yesterday. I did not send him. I have been trying to catch him.”

choices.response: “A collector. He trades in futures — small ones, at first: a song, a voice, a cure, a blade. Each sale bends a timeline a little. Enough small bends, and the whole river changes course.”

choices.text: “Why did you not stop him yourself?”
choices.response: “I am the custodian, not the repairer. I keep the Core; you walk the timelines. That is the division of our labours — and it has held for a very long time.”

n2.text: “The Core is fractured,” the Chronarch says. “Four digits will seal it — one from each act you repaired. The Kite, the Loom, the Lens and the Wing. Speak them in order, and the pedlar's work unravels.”

choices.text: “I have the digits. I will seal the Core.”
choices.response: “Then go to the fracture. And Restorer — whatever you told Franklin in 1764, the Core remembers. Choose your final words with care.”

n1.text: The Chronarch stands at the dais. “The Core is sealed. Now, Restorer — the reckoning. What did you learn, walking through the centuries?”

choices.text: “That history is fragile — and worth protecting.”
choices.response: “Well said. The timeline is not a river to be dammed, nor a toy to be bent. It is a trust. You have kept it.”

choices.text: “That the future should stay in the future.”
choices.response: “Mostly,” the Chronarch says, with the faintest smile. “Though the future arrives soon enough on its own. Your work was to keep it from arriving early.”

magnifier.name: Magnifying Glass
magnifier.desc: A brass magnifying glass. It reveals what the naked eye misses — including hidden ink.

document.name: Historical Document
document.desc: A society letter, written in ordinary ink — and, you suspect, something more.

copper_wire.name: Copper Wire
copper_wire.desc: A spool of fine copper wire. It carries a charge well.

lodestone.name: Lodestone
lodestone.desc: A naturally magnetic stone. It pulls iron to itself and points, roughly, north.

glass_tube.name: Glass Tube
glass_tube.desc: A slender glass tube from the instrument cabinet.

printing_type.name: Printing Type
printing_type.desc: A tray of movable metal type, ready to be set.

candle.name: Tallow Candle
candle.desc: A plain tallow candle — the honest light of 1764.

journal.name: Franklin's Journal Notes
journal.desc: Notes on electricity, in Franklin's hand, with a sketch of the humming device.

brass_key.name: Brass Key

ink_pot.name: Ink Pot
ink_pot.desc: A pot of thick black ink.

sealing_wax.name: Sealing Wax
sealing_wax.desc: Sticks of red sealing wax for letters and documents.

compass.name: Brass Compass
compass.desc: A brass compass. Its needle is steady and true.

hidden_ink_clue.name: Hidden-Ink Clue
hidden_ink_clue.desc: Revealed under the magnifier: 'THE KITE DRAWS THE SPARK. DISCHARGE THE DEVICE WITH THE RESONATOR, AND THE TIMELINE WILL HEAL.' Also, a number: 7.

resonator_coil.name: Resonator Coil

loom_shuttle.name: Loom Shuttle

ledger.name: Delivery Ledger

grounding_wrench.name: Grounding Wrench
grounding_wrench.desc: A wrench wrapped in copper wire — a tool for draining a strange charge safely into the earth.

star_chart.name: Star Chart
star_chart.desc: A hand-drawn chart of the planets.

manuscript.name: Bound Manuscript
manuscript.desc: A bound manuscript of lecture notes, ready for correction.

draft_correction.name: Draft Correction

sealed_correction.name: Sealed Correction
sealed_correction.desc: The corrected chart, sealed with red wax. It can replace the false chart.

flight_log.name: Flight Log
flight_log.desc: The airfield's flight log, recording every takeoff and landing.

spark_plug.name: Spark Plug

fabric_roll.name: Linen Fabric Roll

propeller_blade.name: Wooden Propeller Blade

chronarch_sigil.name: Chronarch's Sigil
chronarch_sigil.desc: A small sigil of the Core. Proof of your deeds.

temporal_key_1.name: Temporal Key — Kite Digit (7)
temporal_key_1.desc: A fragment of sealed time. The number 7 — the Kite Digit, earned in Philadelphia, 1764.

temporal_key_2.name: Temporal Key — Loom Digit (3)
temporal_key_2.desc: A fragment of sealed time. The number 3 — the Loom Digit, earned in Manchester.

temporal_key_3.name: Temporal Key — Lens Digit (1)

recipes.message: Under the magnifier, hidden ink blooms across the letter: 'THE KITE DRAWS THE SPARK. DISCHARGE THE DEVICE WITH THE RESONATOR.' And a number: 7.
You wind the copper wire tight around the lodestone. The coil hums faintly.
You seal the coil inside the glass tube. The Aetheric Resonator is complete — a device of this century's materials, built to discharge the future device.
You wrap the wrench in copper wire. A grounding wrench — a tool for draining a strange charge safely into the earth.
You write the correction in fresh ink: the tiny creatures are real, but their role in disease is not yet proven. The manuscript now tells the truth of its time.
You seal the corrected manuscript with red wax. It is ready to replace the false chart.

press.fact: FACT: Benjamin Franklin ran a successful printing business in Philadelphia from 1728, and published the Pennsylvania Gazette from 1729. Printing was his trade and his fortune.
press.clue: The press is genuine. The distortion is elsewhere.

leyden_jar.fact: FACT: the Leyden jar — a glass jar lined with metal foil that stores static electricity — was invented in 1745–46. Franklin used it in his electrical experiments in the 1750s.

kite_experiment.fact: FACT: Franklin's kite experiment of 1752 demonstrated that lightning is electricity. He did not fly the kite alone in a storm, and he was not struck by lightning — his son William assisted, and they were careful.
kite_experiment.clue: A real experiment — but remember, the kite is not the anomaly.

library_company.fact: FACT: Franklin founded the Library Company of Philadelphia in 1731 — America's first lending library. Members pooled money to buy books they could not afford alone.
library_company.clue: The library belongs here. The lamp inside it does not.

globe_1764.fact: FACT: globes of 1764 showed the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia — with vast blank spaces where the Pacific and the interior of continents were still unmapped.
globe_1764.clue: An honest map of an honestly incomplete world.

franklin_man.fact: FACT: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a printer, scientist, inventor and statesman. In 1764 he was in Philadelphia, already famous for his electrical work.
franklin_man.clue: The man is real. The device has changed him — not the other way around.

printer_man.fact: A fictional character — a master printer of the period. Master printers ran the presses, trained apprentices, and set type by hand.
printer_man.clue: A man of his trade, in his time.

vendor_man.fact: A fictional character — a market vendor of the period. Philadelphia's markets sold iron, cloth, bread and goods from across the Atlantic.
vendor_man.clue: He sold the pedlar's goods without knowing what they were.

apprentice_man.fact: A fictional character — a printer's apprentice. Apprentices lived with their masters, learned the trade over years, and did the heavy work of the shop.
apprentice_man.clue: He noticed the tunes first. Children always notice first.

librarian_woman.fact: A fictional character — a librarian of the Library Company. Lending libraries kept careful catalogues; every book had its place.

music_player.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: portable digital music players appeared in the late 20th century. In 1764 there were no batteries, no transistors, no recorded sound. This object is the anchor of the Act 1 anomaly.
music_player.clue: It hums with stored lightning. It needs a counter-frequency to discharge safely — a resonator built from this century's materials.

plastic_bottle.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: plastics as we know them are a 20th-century invention. A feather-light, perfectly clear bottle could not exist in 1764.
plastic_bottle.clue: One of the pedlar's goods. The pedlar sold tomorrow in three places.

electric_lamp.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: practical electric lamps did not exist until Edison's work in 1879 — more than a century from now. In 1764, light meant flame, candle or oil.
electric_lamp.clue: The lamp appeared the same Tuesday as the music player. Same pedlar, same hand.

power_loom.fact: FACT: Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom in 1785. By the 1830s, steam-driven looms filled Manchester's mills — and the city's population had exploded around them.
power_loom.clue: The looms belong here. The box behind them does not.

cotton_trade.fact: FACT: Manchester's mills ran on cotton grown largely by enslaved labour in the Americas. The industry's wealth, and its human cost, were bound together.
cotton_trade.clue: Remember the cost, not only the machines.

radio_set.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: radio broadcasting began in the early 20th century. In the 1830s there were no radio waves carrying voices — only wires, and not even those for speech.
radio_set.clue: Its heart is a coil. Ground it — drain its charge into the earth through copper — and it will go quiet.

mill_owner_man.fact: A fictional character — a Manchester mill owner of the 1830s. Mill owners built fortunes on steam, cotton and the labour of hundreds.
mill_owner_man.clue: Proud of his machines, frightened of the box.

worker_man.fact: A fictional character — a mill worker. In the 1830s, mill hands worked long hours in dangerous conditions; children worked beside adults until the Factory Act of 1833 began to limit it.
worker_man.clue: Three witnesses, three stories. Only one saw the pedlar clearly.

engineer_woman.fact: A fictional character — a mill engineer. Women engineers were rare in the 1830s, but women worked throughout the mills as spinners, weavers and mechanics.
engineer_woman.clue: She knows machines — and she knows the box is impossible.

telescope.fact: FACT: Newton's reflecting telescope of 1668 used a mirror instead of a lens and opened the heavens. Telescopes transformed astronomy in the 1600s.
telescope.clue: The sky is honest. The chart on the apothecary's wall is not.

microscope.fact: FACT: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's microscopes of the 1670s revealed tiny living things — 'animalcules' — in water and plaque. But no one then connected them to disease.
microscope.clue: Seeing is not understanding. Leeuwenhoek saw the creatures; he did not know what they did.

principia.fact: FACT: Isaac Newton's Principia Mathematica, published in 1687, set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation — the foundation of classical physics.
principia.clue: 1687: the last stone of the arch. The chain is Harvey, Boyle, Leeuwenhoek, Newton.

germ_chart.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: germ theory — the idea that specific microbes cause specific diseases — was not proven until the 1860s, with Pasteur and Lister. A correct germ chart in the 1690s is two centuries too early.
germ_chart.clue: Correct, and impossible. It must be corrected, not burned — write the truth of its time and seal it.

astronomer_man.fact: A fictional character — an astronomer of the late 1600s, working in the new science of Newton and the Royal Society's tradition.
astronomer_man.clue: He knows the order of discovery. Ask him about it.

apothecary_woman.fact: A fictional character — an apothecary and healer. Apothecaries mixed medicines from herbs, minerals and tradition, and were often the first healers the sick would see.
apothecary_woman.clue: She copied the chart in good faith. The fault is the pedlar's, not hers.

student_man.fact: A fictional character — a student of natural philosophy. Universities of the late 1600s taught the new philosophy alongside the old — and argued fiercely about both.
student_man.clue: He has the order right. Listen to him.

biplane.fact: FACT: the Wright brothers first flew a powered aeroplane in 1903. By 1912, biplanes of wood, linen and wire were crossing the English Channel (Blériot, 1909) and carrying mail.
biplane.clue: Wood, linen, wire and a rotary engine. That is a 1912 aeroplane.

blueprint.fact: FACT: early aircraft were designed on paper first — wood frames, linen covering, wire bracing, rotary engines. Every part was accounted for on the blueprint.
blueprint.clue: Every part is accounted for — except the blade.

turbine_blade.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: jet turbine engines were developed in the late 1930s and 1940s (Whittle, von Ohain). A turbine blade bolted to a 1912 biplane is thirty years too early.
turbine_blade.clue: It must be removed with a wrench, in the right order — and the wooden propeller restored.

pilot_woman.fact: A fictional character — a pilot of 1912. Women flew from the earliest days of aviation: Raymonde de Laroche earned the first pilot's licence in 1910.
pilot_woman.clue: She flew with the blade once. Never again.

mechanic_man.fact: A fictional character — an airfield mechanic. Early mechanics built, repaired and flew the machines they maintained, often with little more than hand tools.
mechanic_man.clue: He fitted the blade. He wants it melted down.

engineer4_woman.fact: A fictional character — an aeronautical engineer. Early aviation engineering was done with slide rules and wind tunnels; lift had to exceed weight, thrust had to exceed drag.
engineer4_woman.clue: She did the sums. The blade cannot work on this airframe.

core_fracture.fact: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: the Core is fractured by four acts of interference — one pedlar, four sales, four timelines bent. The fracture is the sum of every anomaly you repaired.
core_fracture.clue: Four key digits seal it: Kite 7, Loom 3, Lens 1, Wing 9.

chronarch_being.fact: A fictional being — custodian of the timelines. Neither young nor old, neither kind nor cruel — only patient.
chronarch_being.clue: The Chronarch keeps the Core. You walk the timelines. That is the division of labours.

stream_1764.fact: FACT: Philadelphia in 1764 was a thriving colonial port — printing, trade, philosophy and the first stirrings of the ideas that would become a revolution.
stream_1764.clue: Steady and bright, since your repair.

stream_mill.fact: FACT: Manchester's mills transformed Britain — and the world — in the 19th century, for good and for ill.
stream_mill.clue: The workers' voices still argue. You chose the true account.

anachronism_workshop.title: What Does Not Belong?
anachronism_workshop.instructions: Look at the objects on the workbench. Three of them do not belong in 1764. Select all three, then confirm.
anachronism_workshop.hint: Ask yourself: could this be made, powered or understood in 1764? Music from a box, light without flame, a bottle lighter than glass — none of these belong.

sequence_franklin.title: Franklin's Milestones
sequence_franklin.instructions: Put Franklin's real milestones in chronological order. Click them in order, from earliest to latest, then confirm.
sequence_franklin.hint: Printing came first — his trade. Then the library. The kite and the lightning rod both belong to the early 1750s, the kite first.

cipher_letter.title: The Traveller's Note
cipher_letter.instructions: The apothecary found this note at the bottom of the false chart. The letters are shifted — decode it to learn the name at the heart of the discovery chain.
cipher_letter.hint: A Caesar shift: each letter marches three places forward in the alphabet. Shift each letter back by three to read it. (Q → N, H → E…)
cipher_letter.encoded: Q H Z W R Q

sequence_loom.title: The Loom's Order
sequence_loom.instructions: Cloth is made in order — always. Put the four stages of making cloth in their correct order, from first to last.
sequence_loom.hint: Raw cotton first. Then carding — combing the fibres straight. Then spinning into thread. Then weaving into cloth.

testimony.title: Three Stories, One Night
testimony.instructions: Three people saw the night the box arrived — and they tell three different stories. Only one account fits all the facts. Choose it.
testimony.hint: Tommy was there at midnight and saw the cart. Martha's 'woman' and Old Jeb's 'no one' do not match the footprints by the mill door — or the coins the pedlar paid with.

statements.text: “A woman brought the box, in daylight, and left it by the door.” — Martha, neighbour
statements.why: Martha was not at the mill that day, and the box arrived at night.

statements.text: “A man with a cart, after midnight. He carried the box in himself and said he was 'from later'.” — Tommy Fletcher
statements.why: Tommy was there. The cart tracks, the midnight hour and the pedlar's own words all agree.

statements.text: “No one brought it. It was simply there in the morning, like dew.” — Old Jeb
statements.why: Jeb sleeps through the night shift. The box did not appear by itself.

sequence_discovery.title: The Chain of Discovery
sequence_discovery.instructions: Discovery has an order — each great finding stands on the one before. Put the four discoveries in chronological order.
sequence_discovery.hint: Harvey's blood (1628) first. Then Boyle's air (1662). Then Leeuwenhoek's tiny creatures (1670s). Then Newton's laws (1687).

parts_pick.title: What Belongs on a 1912 Biplane?
parts_pick.instructions: Six parts lie on the bench. Three belong on a 1912 biplane. Three do not. Select the three that belong, then confirm.
parts_pick.hint: A 1912 aeroplane is wood, linen, wire and a rotary engine. Anything of gleaming alloy, jet fuel or radar does not belong.

sequence_assembly.title: Build Her in Order
sequence_assembly.instructions: A machine is built in order — and unbuilt in order. Put the four stages of assembling the biplane in their correct order.
sequence_assembly.hint: Frame first — the skeleton. Then the wings. Then the engine. Last, the propeller.

memory_recall.title: The Order of Ages
memory_recall.instructions: The Core asks you to remember. Put the four eras you visited in chronological order, from earliest to latest.
memory_recall.hint: The scholars of the 1690s came first. Then Franklin's Philadelphia. Then the mills. Last, the airfield.

final_code.title: Seal the Core
final_code.instructions: Four key digits — one from each act you repaired. Enter them in order: Kite, Loom, Lens, Wing.
final_code.hint: The Kite Digit is 7 (the hidden-ink clue in Philadelphia). The Loom Digit is 3. The Lens Digit is 1. The Wing Digit is 9. Together: 7319.

questions.q: What was Benjamin Franklin's main trade in Philadelphia?
questions.explanation: FACT: Franklin ran a successful printing business in Philadelphia from 1728, publishing the Pennsylvania Gazette from 1729.

questions.q: In which year did Franklin help found the Library Company of Philadelphia?
questions.explanation: FACT: the Library Company was founded in 1731 — America's first lending library.

questions.q: What did Franklin's kite experiment of 1752 demonstrate?
options: That kites can fly in rain
That lightning is caused by the moon
That electricity comes from the sun
questions.explanation: FACT: the 1752 kite experiment showed that lightning is electricity.

questions.q: What did Franklin devise to protect buildings from lightning?
questions.explanation: FACT: Franklin devised the lightning rod in 1752–53.

questions.q: Which of these did NOT exist in 1764?
questions.explanation: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: plastics are a 20th-century invention. The other three were everyday objects in 1764.

questions.q: In which year did the Liverpool and Manchester Railway open?
questions.explanation: FACT: the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830 — the world's first inter-city railway.

questions.q: Who patented the power loom, and when?
questions.explanation: FACT: Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom in 1785.

questions.q: What did the Factory Act of 1833 begin to limit?
questions.explanation: FACT: the Factory Act of 1833 began to limit child labour in textile mills.

questions.q: What powered Manchester's mills in the 1830s?
questions.explanation: FACT: steam engines — Watt's improved engine from 1776 — powered the mills.

questions.q: What is the correct order of making cloth?
questions.explanation: FACT: raw cotton, then carding, then spinning into thread, then weaving into cloth.

questions.q: In which year was Newton's Principia published?
questions.explanation: FACT: the Principia Mathematica was published in 1687.

questions.q: Who first described the circulation of the blood?
questions.explanation: FACT: William Harvey described the circulation of the blood in 1628.

questions.q: What did Leeuwenhoek's microscopes reveal in the 1670s?
questions.explanation: FACT: Leeuwenhoek saw tiny living creatures — 'animalcules' — but did not connect them to disease.

questions.q: What did Boyle's law of 1662 describe?
options: The relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas
questions.explanation: FACT: Boyle's law relates the pressure and volume of a gas at fixed temperature.

questions.q: When was germ theory proven?
questions.explanation: FACT: germ theory was proven in the 1860s, with Pasteur and Lister — two centuries after the chart in the apothecary.

questions.q: In what year did the Wright brothers first fly a powered aeroplane?
questions.explanation: FACT: the Wright brothers first flew at Kitty Hawk in 1903.

questions.q: Who was first to fly across the English Channel?
questions.explanation: FACT: Louis Blériot crossed the Channel in 1909.

questions.q: What were early aeroplanes mostly made of?
questions.explanation: FACT: early aeroplanes were wood frames covered in linen, braced with wire.

questions.q: The turbine blade in the hangar belonged to which era?
questions.explanation: ALTERNATE TIMELINE: jet turbine engines were developed in the late 1930s and 1940s — thirty years after 1912.

questions.q: What must lift exceed for an aeroplane to fly?
questions.explanation: FACT: lift must exceed weight, and thrust must exceed drag.

act5.title: Act 5 — Historical Verification: The Whole Timeline

questions.q: Which came first: the Library Company (1731) or the power loom patent (1785)?
options: They happened in the same year
questions.explanation: FACT: the Library Company (1731) came more than fifty years before Cartwright's power loom (1785).

questions.q: Which of these discoveries came last?
options: They all came in the same century
questions.explanation: FACT: germ theory (1860s) came nearly two centuries after Newton.

questions.q: In what year did Franklin's kite experiment take place?
questions.explanation: FACT: the kite experiment was in 1752.

questions.q: Which of these is a fictional character in this game?
questions.explanation: The Chronarch is fictional. Franklin, Newton and Cartwright were real historical figures.

questions.q: What is the correct chronological order of the four eras you visited?
questions.explanation: FACT: the scholars (1690s), then Philadelphia (1764), then the mills (1830s), then the airfield (1912).

questions.q: Put these in chronological order: Principia (1687), kite experiment (1752), germ theory (1860s), first powered flight (1903).
questions.explanation: FACT: 1687, 1752, 1860s, 1903 — the true order of the chain.

questions.q: Which of these appeared first in history?
questions.explanation: FACT: Franklin's printing business (1728) predates the power loom (1785) by more than fifty years.

questions.q: What did the pedlar sell in every act?
options: Nothing — he was only a rumour
questions.explanation: In every act, the same pedlar sold tomorrow to yesterday: a song, a voice, a cure, a blade.

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE about this game?
options: Everything in the game is historical fact
The pedlar is a real historical figure
The Chronarch and the pedlar are fictional; Franklin, Newton and the Wrights are real
questions.explanation: The Chronarch, the pedlar and the other townsfolk are fictional. Franklin, Newton, Cartwright, Harvey, Boyle, Leeuwenhoek and the Wright brothers were real.

questions.q: What seals the Temporal Core?
options: Four key digits, one from each act
questions.explanation: The Kite Digit (7), the Loom Digit (3), the Lens Digit (1) and the Wing Digit (9) — one from each act you repaired.

timelineEvents.text: 1764 — The music player is silenced. Philadelphia's timeline steadies.
RIPPLE: Franklin was told of the future. In later eras, technology arrives slightly early — the Chronarch notes it.
RIPPLE: Franklin was told of electric light. The lamp in the library glows of its own accord — a warning.
1830s — The radio is grounded. The mill's timeline steadies.
1690s — The false chart is corrected and sealed. The chain of discovery is restored.
1912 — The turbine blade is removed. The biplane flies as it was meant to.
Outside time — The Core is sealed with four digits. The pedlar's work unravels.

repairReqs.1: Solve “What Does Not Belong?” in the workshop, then combine a magnifying glass with a historical document to reveal the hidden-ink clue, build the resonator (copper wire + lodestone + glass tube), and USE the resonator on the music player.
repairReqs.2: Solve the loom sequence and the testimony puzzle, then craft the grounding wrench (wrench + copper wire) and USE it on the radio.
repairReqs.3: Solve the discovery sequence and decode the cipher letter, then prepare the sealed correction (draft correction + sealing wax) and USE it on the germ chart.
repairReqs.4: Solve the parts pick and the assembly sequence, then USE the wrench on the turbine blade.
repairReqs.5: The Core is sealed with the four-key code (Kite, Loom, Lens, Wing) and the memory of your journey. INTERACT with the fractured Core.
